A data story · U.S. meat prices, 2015–2026
Why does meat cost so much now?
What happened to beef, pork and chicken prices, which events really mattered, and who got the money.
Scott Schirkofsky · Data through September 2026 · schirko.com/scott/meat-prices
The hook
Ground beef is up 63% since 2015. Prices in general are up 42%.
U.S. average retail prices (Bureau of Labor Statistics) and the Consumer Price Index, monthly, 2015–2026.

The events people blame
Of 16 events, only the COVID closures clearly moved all three meats.
Each dot: how far the price ran from where it was heading, over the six months after the event (notebook 11).
7
Popular claims, checked
The explanations people repeat don't line up with the prices.
“Food plant fires”
Lines up only with chicken's 2022 spike. Beef and pork, which the claim also covers, didn't move.
Doesn't hold up
Colorado bird-flu culls
Came in an ordinary month for chicken prices, which were drifting down at the time.
Doesn't hold up
Cage-free egg law
An ordinary month for chicken breast prices; no jump.
Doesn't hold up
8
The real cause
Drought → ranchers sell cows → smaller herd → higher prices.
More drought, more cows sold. A drier year means about 245,000 more cows sold — that same year, not later.
About 1 in 10. Ranchers can sell that share of the herd each year and keep it steady, because young females replace them. Sell more and the herd shrinks.
1% fewer cows → 1.8% higher price. People keep buying beef when it gets dearer, so the price climbs until enough buyers cut back.
Sources: U.S. Drought Monitor, USDA NASS, BLS; notebook 12. The same chain ran after the 2011–2013 drought.

With an ordinary 2020–2023 drought, beef would have cost about 11 percentage points less in 2025.
10
Who got the money
Ranchers got most of beef's increase. Packers got less.
+$2.08
Ranchers — 86% of the rise since 2019. Scarce cattle sell for more.
+$1.13
Stores — most of it in 2026 alone. Pays for wages and rent as well as profit.
−$0.81
Packers — squeezed from $1.11 to $0.30 a pound by record cattle prices.
Each step's part of a pound of fresh beef, in September 2026 dollars. Source: USDA ERS price spreads; notebook 13.

12
What to watch next
In 2026, ranchers are keeping their cows despite the drought.
Now
Drought is almost as widespread as in 2022, yet the fewest cows in the data are going to slaughter.
Next year
Keeping cows rebuilds the herd, but it keeps beef scarce at first: cows kept for breeding aren't turned into beef.
The signal
The January 2027 herd count, and whether beef's 2026 gap above the shortage's prediction closes.
13
Appendix · How it was done
Free government data, tested honestly, refreshed with one command.
Data
Retail prices and inflation (BLS); price spreads, cattle herd and slaughter (USDA); drought (U.S. Drought Monitor). Monthly, 2010 on.
Honesty checks
Every result compared with ordinary months. The first method would have flagged 30% of ordinary months as “events”; this test caught it.
Limits
National averages. 12–16 years per measurement. Overlapping events can't be separated. Price spreads include costs as well as profit.
Notebooks, findings guide and an interactive explorer: schirko.com/scott/meat-prices
